content.title: About
content.content: Cannelloni are large pasta tubes stuffed with a cheese and spinach mixture. In this version they are served without sauce, allowing the delicate flavor of the filling and the texture of the pasta to shine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cannelloni originate from Italy, where they are traditionally baked with a tomato sauce.
The cheese‑spinach combination provides a good balance of protein, calcium and iron.
The pasta dough is usually made from durum wheat, giving it a firm bite after cooking.
Without sauce, cannelloni are often drizzled with olive oil, fresh herbs, or a light balsamic glaze.
The sauce‑free version is popular among those watching sugar intake and overall calories.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The cheese filling supplies high‑quality protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Cheese provides calcium that supports bone and tooth health.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Spinach offers non‑heme iron, important for blood formation.

items.title: Low in added sugars
items.content: Skipping the sauce reduces added sugars, beneficial for blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Both cheese and spinach contain B2, B6 and folate, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cheese may cause discomfort for people who cannot digest lactose.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to dairy proteins.

items.title: Oxalates in spinach
items.content: Spinach contains oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible persons.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheeses often contain salt; those monitoring sodium intake should account for it.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the cannelloni hot, drizzled with a little olive oil and sprinkled with fresh herbs. They are eaten with a fork and knife, cutting the tubes in half if desired. A light tomato puree or avocado mash can be added for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked cannelloni in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Frozen portions retain quality for up to 2 months; thaw in the fridge before reheating.

content.title: About
content.content: Gluten‑free French toast is a classic dish made from slices of gluten‑free bread dipped in a mixture of eggs, milk (or a plant‑based alternative) and spices, then fried until golden. The gluten‑free version makes it safe for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The traditional French toast originated in France in the 17th century and was called “pain perdu” (lost bread).
The gluten‑free version appeared in the early 2000s as demand for gluten‑free products surged.
Gluten‑free breads often use blends of rice, corn and potato flours.
French toast is commonly served with maple syrup, berries, nuts or yogurt.
Both sweet and savory versions exist; savory versions may include cheese, ham or vegetables.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Eggs and milk (or their plant‑based counterparts) provide a substantial amount of complete protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: B2 and B12 vitamins found in eggs and fortified gluten‑free milk support energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Gluten‑free breads are often fortified with iron, helping maintain normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Lower glycemic index with whole‑grain gluten‑free breads
items.content: Whole‑grain gluten‑free breads release sugar more slowly, which can aid blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Adding fruit or berries increases fiber content, promoting healthy gut function.

items.title: Egg or milk allergy
items.content: People allergic to eggs, dairy or their plant‑based substitutes should use alternative ingredients.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Toppings like maple syrup or powdered sugar can significantly raise calories and sugar levels.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: French toast, especially when cooked with butter and served with syrup, can be energy‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Only use certified gluten‑free bread to avoid accidental gluten exposure.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Whisk eggs with milk (or plant‑based alternative), add a pinch of salt, cinnamon and vanilla. Dip gluten‑free bread slices, let them soak, then fry in a lightly oiled pan until golden on both sides. Serve hot with berries, nuts, yogurt or maple syrup.

content.title: Storage
content.content: French toast is best enjoyed fresh. Leftovers can be cooled to room temperature, then stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in a skillet or oven to restore crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate gelato is an Italian frozen dessert made from milk, cream, sugar, and high‑quality cocoa. The slow‑churn process gives gelato a denser, more aromatic texture than regular ice cream, with a rich chocolate flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Gelato contains less air than traditional ice cream, resulting in a creamier mouthfeel.
It is typically served at about -12°C, whereas ice cream is stored around -18°C.
Italian gelato makers often use dark chocolate with 70%+ cocoa content for a deep flavor.
Unlike many ice creams, gelato usually does not contain emulsifiers or stabilizers.
The first references to gelato date back to the 16th century in Italy.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Cocoa is rich in flavonoids that help combat free radicals and support heart health.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium in cocoa supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Provides calcium
items.content: The dairy base supplies calcium essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Cream contributes monounsaturated fats, which can be heart‑friendly in moderation.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Gelato quickly replenishes energy thanks to its blend of carbohydrates and fats.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Gelato contains milk and cream, which may trigger reactions in people allergic to lactose or casein.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The sweet dessert can raise blood glucose levels, so those with diabetes should limit portions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Gelato is energy‑dense; excessive consumption may contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Caffeine and theobromine
items.content: Cocoa contains small amounts of theobromine, which can affect sleep and heart rate in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy gelato with a spoon, in a waffle cone, or paired with fruit, nuts, and sauces. For extra depth, sprinkle a pinch of sea salt or fresh berries on top.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store gelato in the freezer at about -12°C in an airtight container to prevent ice crystal formation. Let it sit 2–3 minutes at room temperature before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: The Light Ice Cream Bar with vanilla flavor is a low‑calorie dessert made from skimmed milk, natural vanilla flavoring, and a small amount of sweeteners. It has a smooth, creamy texture and a pronounced vanilla aroma while containing minimal fat and sugar.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The bar is marketed as “light,” containing roughly 2‑3 times fewer calories than regular ice‑cream bars.
The vanilla flavor is derived from natural extracts rather than artificial aromatics.
Each bar is packaged in an individual aluminum wrapper that preserves freshness and protects from light.
The product is often used in sports nutrition as a quick source of carbohydrates after training.

items.title: Low Fat Content
items.content: The bar contains less than 1 g of fat per 100 g, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of Calcium
items.content: Skimmed milk provides about 10 % of the daily calcium requirement, important for bone health.

items.title: B‑Vitamins
items.content: It supplies small amounts of vitamins B2 and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Low Glycemic Index
items.content: Sweeteners with a low glycemic index help avoid rapid blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Milk Protein Allergy
items.content: The product contains milk protein and may trigger reactions in individuals allergic to dairy.

items.title: Sweetener Content
items.content: Artificial sweeteners used to reduce calories can cause discomfort in sensitive people.

items.title: Storage at High Temperatures
items.content: If kept above ‑10 °C for extended periods, the bar may melt and lose its texture.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Keep the bar frozen and consume it straight from the freezer. It can be enjoyed as a standalone treat or added to smoothies for extra flavor and light sweetness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store at ‑18 °C or lower. After removal from the wrapper, do not leave at room temperature for more than 10 minutes, otherwise the texture may change.

content.title: About
content.content: Pistachios are the edible seeds of the pistachio tree (Pistacia vera), native to the Mediterranean region, Iran, the United States and other warm climates. Salting gives them a distinctive salty flavor, while their crunchy texture makes them a popular snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pistachios belong to the Anacardiaceae family and are close relatives of cashews and mangoes.
About 70 % of the world’s pistachios are grown in Iran and the United States (California).
Pistachios split open only when fully ripe; unripe nuts remain closed.
Traditionally they are eaten as a snack and used in confectionery, ice cream and pastes.
Salt is usually added after roasting to preserve the nut’s natural aroma.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Pistachios contain vitamin E, polyphenols and carotenoids that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: The majority of fat in pistachios is monounsaturated, which supports heart health.

items.title: Source of protein and fiber
items.content: One cup (≈ 150 g) of pistachios provides about 20 g of protein and 10 g of dietary fiber, promoting satiety.

items.title: Contains essential minerals
items.content: Pistachios are a good source of potassium, magnesium and phosphorus, important for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Supports gut microbiota
items.content: Prebiotic fibers in pistachios foster the growth of beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Pistachios can trigger severe allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to nuts.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Salted pistachios contain a notable amount of sodium; people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Pistachios are calorie‑rich, so portion sizes should be moderate, especially for weight management.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Whole pistachios can pose a choking risk for young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pistachios can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, added to salads, yogurts, oatmeal, baked goods, or processed into pistachio butter. They are often lightly roasted and then sprinkled with sea salt before consumption.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pistachios in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from light. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation.
